e-7347.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Centered at the Origin
e-7347.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/1782385c55493892be0308ede1e4fbe5308ea9440e21b70cc2da7d7f01fb8dcd.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is $\displaystyle \iint\limits_D y \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
e-7347.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

e-7346.knowledge_point: Evaluating Repeated Integrals Expressed in Polar Coordinates
e-7346.worked_solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{[{r}^{2}]}_{0}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the double-angle formula

$$
\cos{2x} = 1-2\sin^2 x.
$$

Substituting $x=2\theta$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\sin^22\theta = \dfrac12\left(1-\cos4\theta\right).
$$

 

Finally, we can finish our integral by integrating with respect to $\theta,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\theta -\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(0-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{2}{8}) \\  & =\frac{1}{32}(\pi -2)\end{aligned}
$$

e-7348.problem: Integrate the function $f(x, y) = 15xy^2$ over the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $x \geq 0,y \geq 0.$
e-7348.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D\mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/051cfbbf3fd37f01ff7e4442fccdc5ec4ce506e3c452b68bfa2ed5ae6e5cf6b9.png)

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 2, \:0\leq \theta \leq  \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}15x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}15r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,{[{r}^{5}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({2}^{5}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =32{[{sin}^{3}⁡\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =32({sin}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-{sin}^{3}⁡(0)) \\  & =32(1-0) \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

The region D is the circle shown above. What is ∬D(x2−y2)dA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫02π∫02r3cos⁡2θdrdθ
b
∫02π∫04r3cos⁡2θdrdθ
c
∫02π∫02r3drdθ
d
∫02π∫02r2drdθ
e
∫0π∫04r2cos⁡2θdrdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The disk has polar bounds 0 ≤ r ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. Since x² − y² = r²(cos²θ − sin²θ) = r²cos(2θ) and dA = r dr dθ, the transformed integrand is r³cos(2θ). Thus option a expresses the integral over the given region.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/cdd5f0c58228b47a0bbba77daf2b426ce0247e71259e2b5af1a4a80fa833a036.png)

The region $D$ is the circle shown above. What is ${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

The region D is the circle shown above. What is ∬D(x2−y2)dA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫02π∫02r3cos⁡2θdrdθ
b
∫02π∫04r3cos⁡2θdrdθ
c
∫02π∫02r3drdθ
d
∫02π∫02r2drdθ
e
∫0π∫04r2cos⁡2θdrdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬Δf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ.

First, notice that the region D represents the disk of radius 2 centered at the origin. In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region can be expressed as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤2,0≤θ≤2π}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain
∬D(x2−y2)dA=∬Δ((rcos⁡θ)2−(rsin⁡θ)2)rdrdθ=∫02π∫02r3(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)drdθ=∫02π∫02r3cos⁡2θdrdθ.

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Centered at the Origin
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/cdd5f0c58228b47a0bbba77daf2b426ce0247e71259e2b5af1a4a80fa833a036.png)

The region $D$ is the circle shown above. What is ${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

The region D is the quarter-circle shown above. What is ∬D(x2+y2)dA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫0π/2∫02r2drdθ
b
∫3π/20∫01r2drdθ
c
∫−π/20∫02rdrdθ
d
∫−π/20∫02r3drdθ
e
∫−π/20∫01r3drdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The region is the fourth-quadrant disk sector with 0 ≤ r ≤ 2 and −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 0. Since x² + y² = r² and dA = r dr dθ, the integrand becomes r³, giving option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/8c3056de2634d5315aebcbc978bf279eeb95da736ab6796c9d86dc39d9feadc5.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

The region D is the quarter-circle shown above. What is ∬D(x2+y2)dA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫0π/2∫02r2drdθ
b
∫3π/20∫01r2drdθ
c
∫−π/20∫02rdrdθ
d
∫−π/20∫02r3drdθ
e
∫−π/20∫01r3drdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

First, notice that the region D represents a portion of the disk of radius 2 centered at the origin. In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region can be expressed as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤2,−π2≤θ≤0}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∬D(x2+y2)dA=∬Δ((rcos⁡θ)2+(rsin⁡θ)2)rdrdθ=∫−π/20∫02r3(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)drdθ=∫−π/20∫02r3drdθ.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d: the fourth-quadrant sector has 0 ≤ r ≤ 2 and −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 0. Substituting x² + y² = r² and dA = r dr dθ gives r³ dr dθ. The incorrect feedback concerns a deliberately submitted option a, not option d.

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Centered at the Origin
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/8c3056de2634d5315aebcbc978bf279eeb95da736ab6796c9d86dc39d9feadc5.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

The region D is the quarter-circle shown above. What is ∬Dex2+y2dA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫π/23π/2∫04rer2drdθ
b
∫π3π/2∫02er2drdθ
c
∫π3π/2∫04rerdrdθ
d
∫π/23π/2∫02r2erdrdθ
e
∫π3π/2∫04rer2drdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The region is a third-quadrant quarter-disk of radius 4, so 0 ≤ r ≤ 4 and π ≤ θ ≤ 3π/2. Since x² + y² = r² and dA = r dr dθ, the transformed integrand is r e^(r²). This gives option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/aa5b04b98d3796656fca912d8dc1732ea7e12bab9083f8ca543ad5fd4fdb10ff.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is ${∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $4$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4}r{e}^{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

The region D is the quarter-circle shown above. What is ∬Dex2+y2dA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫π/23π/2∫04rer2drdθ
b
∫π3π/2∫02er2drdθ
c
∫π3π/2∫04rerdrdθ
d
∫π/23π/2∫02r2erdrdθ
e
∫π3π/2∫04rer2drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

First, notice that the region D represents a portion of the disk of radius 4 centered at the origin. In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region can be expressed as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,π≤θ≤3π2}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain
∬Dex2+y2dA=∬Δe(rcos⁡θ)2+(rsin⁡θ)2rdrdθ=∫π3π/2∫04rer2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)drdθ=∫π3π/2∫04rer2drdθ.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/aa5b04b98d3796656fca912d8dc1732ea7e12bab9083f8ca543ad5fd4fdb10ff.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is ${∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $4$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4}r{e}^{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

The region D is the circle shown above. What is ∬Dln⁡(x2+y2+1)dA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫02π∫04ln⁡(r+1)drdθ
b
∫0π∫016ln⁡(r2+1)drdθ
c
∫02π∫016r2ln⁡(r+1)drdθ
d
∫02π∫04rln⁡(r2+1)drdθ
e

Submit

decision.explanation: The disk x² + y² ≤ 16 has polar bounds 0 ≤ r ≤ 4 and 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. Using x² + y² = r² and dA = r dr dθ gives the integrand r ln(r² + 1), so option d is correct.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/6b077d20bcb79f293383a7810d1c46ad42ce78d17a8d631b01f66a9fd547f475.png)

The region $D$ is the circle shown above. What is ${∬}_{D}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $4$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1)r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+1)\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

a

b
∫0π∫016ln⁡(r2+1)drdθ

∫02π∫016r2ln⁡(r+1)drdθ

EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form ∬Df(x,y)dA=∬Δf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/6b077d20bcb79f293383a7810d1c46ad42ce78d17a8d631b01f66a9fd547f475.png)

The region $D$ is the circle shown above. What is ${∬}_{D}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $4$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1)r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+1)\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4}r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

The region D is the semicircle shown above. What is ∬D2xydA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫0π/2∫02r2sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2∫01r2sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
c
∫0π/2∫02r3sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
d
∫−π/2π/2∫02r3sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
e
∫−π/2π/2∫02r2sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The right semicircle has bounds 0 ≤ r ≤ 2 and −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Since 2xy = 2r²cos(θ)sin(θ) = r²sin(2θ) and dA = r dr dθ, the transformed integrand is r³sin(2θ). Thus option d gives the required polar-coordinate expression.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/bccbe3973fa63908f5e264f4566e1207c5019dc1de9c36ef42481428527aef3b.png)

The region $D$ is the semicircle shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

The region D is the semicircle shown above. What is ∬D2xydA expressed in polar coordinates?

a
∫0π/2∫02r2sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
b
∫−π/2π/2∫01r2sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
c
∫0π/2∫02r3sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
d
∫−π/2π/2∫02r3sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
e
∫−π/2π/2∫02r2sin⁡(2θ)drdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

First, notice that the region D represents a portion of the disk of radius 2 centered at the origin. In polar coordinates (r,θ), the region can be expressed as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤2,−π2≤θ≤π2}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∬D2xydA=∬Δ2(rcos⁡θ)(rsin⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫−π/2π/2∫022r3sin⁡θcos⁡θdrdθ=∫−π/2π/2∫02r3sin⁡(2θ)drdθ.

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Centered at the Origin
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/bccbe3973fa63908f5e264f4566e1207c5019dc1de9c36ef42481428527aef3b.png)

The region $D$ is the semicircle shown above. What is
${∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A$
expressed in polar coordinates?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

If D={(x,y):x2+(y−2)2≤4,x≥0}, then ∬Dx2+y2dA=

a
∫0π/2∫04sin⁡θr2drdθ
b
∫0π∫04sin⁡θr2drdθ
c
∫0π/2∫02sin⁡θr2drdθ

Submit

decision.explanation: The disk inequality becomes r² − 4r sin(θ) ≤ 0, giving 0 ≤ r ≤ 4 sin(θ). The restriction x ≥ 0 selects 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Since √(x² + y²) = r and dA = r dr dθ, the transformed integrand is r². Thus option a is correct.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/968419bad65410864c75e8abe766d21ac4d4acd835c73ea84118cf21ac066f79.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4 & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/2fe33fb6e1be8b6107cb667e9453613af906bd4da7d67f9d9323d49cce5ae06c.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/e2b5e7b4433cbfb50ac7a9f991e4e4bc0cf8deecfefeeef0a4c9606ab6183cce.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the region D represents a portion of the disk of radius 2 centered at (0,2).

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

{x=rcos⁡θy=rsin⁡θ

With that in mind, let's now write the x2+(y−2)2=4 in polar coordinates:

x2+(y−2)2=4(rcos⁡θ)2+(rsin⁡θ−2)2=4r2cos2⁡θ+r2sin2⁡θ−4rsin⁡θ+4=4r2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)−4rsin⁡θ=0r2−4rsin⁡θ=0r(r−4sin⁡θ)=0

Since r cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have r=4sin⁡θ.

Now, let's determine the limits for r and θ. First of all, r can vary from r=0 (at the origin) to r=4sin⁡θ (at the boundary of the region):

Secondly, θ can vary between θ=0 (the positive x-axis) and θ=π2 (the positive y-axis):

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin
content.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/968419bad65410864c75e8abe766d21ac4d4acd835c73ea84118cf21ac066f79.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4 & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/2fe33fb6e1be8b6107cb667e9453613af906bd4da7d67f9d9323d49cce5ae06c.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/e2b5e7b4433cbfb50ac7a9f991e4e4bc0cf8deecfefeeef0a4c9606ab6183cce.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The disk inequality becomes r² − 2r cos(θ) ≤ 0, so 0 ≤ r ≤ 2cos(θ). Its lower half has −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 0. Using x² + y² = r² and dA = r dr dθ gives r ln(r² + 1), matching option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/bf84eed655256e63439ca907610c4b0b022c6c480d5ab0b6c12d6826af9f0907.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(1,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/6de2b6e2b9925577f8cf0961f8466707f770ddca175a04dac9b592542aac16e8.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis) and $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/4a56d4023b03b40b4c1be5f22809963d6c745fd90ed3d860cf69d555b3e869ae.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+1)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin
content.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/bf84eed655256e63439ca907610c4b0b022c6c480d5ab0b6c12d6826af9f0907.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(1,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/6de2b6e2b9925577f8cf0961f8466707f770ddca175a04dac9b592542aac16e8.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis) and $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/4a56d4023b03b40b4c1be5f22809963d6c745fd90ed3d860cf69d555b3e869ae.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 0}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{ln}⁡((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+1)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r\operatorname{ln}⁡({r}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

If D={(x,y):(x−4)2+y2≤16,y≤0}, then ∬Dex2−y2dA=

a
∫3π/22π∫08cos⁡θer2drdθ
b
∫02π∫08cos⁡θer2cos⁡2θdrdθ
c
∫02π∫04rer2drdθ
d
∫3π/22π∫04rer2cos⁡2θdrdθ
e
∫3π/22π∫08cos⁡θrer2cos⁡2θdrdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: The disk inequality becomes r² − 8r cos(θ) ≤ 0, giving 0 ≤ r ≤ 8cos(θ). Its lower half is described by 3π/2 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. Since x² − y² = r²cos(2θ) and dA = r dr dθ, the transformed integrand is r e^(r²cos(2θ)), matching option e.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/d882bf70ecb7b94eee0eeeffbf63874ca8607268167f96278deb4678ec3b827a.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $4$ centered at $(4,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-4)^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =16 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =16 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -8r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =16 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-8r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-8r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/55c9ea38874993dd10f03061fc3739ec6d7cb8af5b0467d5060a74a5ec22393a.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis) and $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/b845816016bbc646e88af59bd02602b2e1127edfbc22ca82d1fb4e52cc63b41a.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r{e}^{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r{e}^{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r{e}^{{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin
content.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/d882bf70ecb7b94eee0eeeffbf63874ca8607268167f96278deb4678ec3b827a.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $4$ centered at $(4,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-4)^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =16 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =16 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -8r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =16 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-8r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-8r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/55c9ea38874993dd10f03061fc3739ec6d7cb8af5b0467d5060a74a5ec22393a.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis) and $\theta =0$ (the positive $x$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/b845816016bbc646e88af59bd02602b2e1127edfbc22ca82d1fb4e52cc63b41a.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r{e}^{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r{e}^{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }r{e}^{{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Expanding the disk inequality gives x² + y² + x ≤ 0, or r² + r cos(θ) ≤ 0. Thus 0 ≤ r ≤ −cos(θ), and the lower-left half has π ≤ θ ≤ 3π/2. Also, xy² dA = (r cos(θ))(r² sin²(θ))r dr dθ = r⁴ cos(θ)sin²(θ) dr dθ, matching option d.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/617a69d44661d03e1c170b0c397d11f6437a7222c286df5023154371ec90ab4d.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(-\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$ 

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/fe82880fec605db684a2b5cb0da5c88a38da5b4fb4faad1f80c4d5b0691fde21.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =\pi $ (the negative $x$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/9e1693005c8930a7b2b8a3b47bc96f5441bf72ee6c5b67f3b8c97d87cfa2e34b.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin
content.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/617a69d44661d03e1c170b0c397d11f6437a7222c286df5023154371ec90ab4d.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\frac{1}{2}$ centered at $(-\frac{1}{2},0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$ 

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/fe82880fec605db684a2b5cb0da5c88a38da5b4fb4faad1f80c4d5b0691fde21.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =\pi $ (the negative $x$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/9e1693005c8930a7b2b8a3b47bc96f5441bf72ee6c5b67f3b8c97d87cfa2e34b.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\pi \le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The disk inequality becomes r² − 4r cos(θ) ≤ 0, giving 0 ≤ r ≤ 4cos(θ) and −π/2 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Substituting x = r cos(θ), y = r sin(θ), and dA = r dr dθ gives r⁴cos²(θ)sin(θ), matching option b. Other choices may also evaluate to zero by symmetry, but b directly expresses the given domain and transformed integrand.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/86036fd86096355b969da695f812c9bf835880edd68f7991183b70a6234e3eb4.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(2,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/0cf12dd41cddb943fe8b0950cdf13a0480cfbf2620a59d8bc4e8ba8775e0e6c1.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/cf2f0a011734a56f59cce2164a82d745c84b28d1bf706531deb80bb6e0a32640.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Not Centered at the Origin
content.worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/86036fd86096355b969da695f812c9bf835880edd68f7991183b70a6234e3eb4.png)

Notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(2,0).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-2)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2)}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} & =4 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire circle, we must have $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

Now, let's determine the limits for $r$ and $\theta .$ First of all, $r$ can vary from $r=0$ (at the origin) to $r=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ (at the boundary of the region): 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/0cf12dd41cddb943fe8b0950cdf13a0480cfbf2620a59d8bc4e8ba8775e0e6c1.png)

Secondly, $\theta $ can vary between $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the negative $y$-axis) and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{2}$ (the positive $y$-axis):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/cf2f0a011734a56f59cce2164a82d745c84b28d1bf706531deb80bb6e0a32640.png)

So, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Evaluate 
${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{1}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .$
after.worked_solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{1}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]_{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({1}^{2}-(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & ={[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{4}\theta -\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-0 \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{8}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{8-\pi }{8}\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating Repeated Integrals Expressed in Polar Coordinates
content.problem:
Evaluate 
${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{1}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .$
content.worked_solution:
First, we integrate with respect to $r,$ treating $\theta $ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{1}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]_{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}({1}^{2}-(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we integrate with respect to $\theta :$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & ={[\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{4}\theta -\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )-0 \\  & =1-\frac{\pi }{8}-\frac{1}{8}\cdot 0 \\  & =\frac{8-\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)=2x+y$ over the portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin, where $y\ge 0.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/b5ba69ab02aa13e201b7b9113f6a36e705ad19e6412499504afc4f239459a8f3.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )(\frac{{2}^{3}}{3}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{8}{3}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{8}{3}((2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ))-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{16}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The boundary x² + y² = 2y becomes r = 2sin(θ), with 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2. Thus the integral is ∫₀^(π/2)∫₀^(2sinθ) r cot(θ) dr dθ = ∫₀^(π/2) 2sin(θ)cos(θ) dθ = 1. The singularity at the origin is integrable.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/719f86db69489f62bcbe2753e88cdc6713f04dc6f53415cc2484e2eaab8ffac3.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is the semicircle shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(0,1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2} & =2y-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Double Integral by Converting To Polar Coordinates
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/719f86db69489f62bcbe2753e88cdc6713f04dc6f53415cc2484e2eaab8ffac3.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is the semicircle shown above.
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at 
$(0,1).$

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write the $x=\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}}$ in polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2y-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2} & =2y-{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2y \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2} & =2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$

Therefore, in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -0)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-1-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Integrate the function $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ over the disk of radius $2$ centered at the origin.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/811cfa127ad232e8d5a990998604718a57344d1bd7f43173dc0987631c13db33.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{(r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}r{e}^{{r}^{2}}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{1}{2}{e}^{{r}^{2}}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1)[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{4}-1)(2\pi -0) \\  & =\pi ({e}^{4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

First, let's sketch our region $D:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14054995/assets/0a1de805051eff4ea82b4eefb7bb113c724b3d4e7304704831b6294ee4e4d674.png)

In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2({(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2})\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}2{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\frac{81}{4}-0)\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{81}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{81}{2}(2\pi -0) \\  & =81\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
